title: Paper clay sculpted lighthouse
subtitle: A coil-and-slab lighthouse in paper clay, 20 cm tall with cut window openings
excerpt: A lighthouse sculpture is a coil-built tower with a slab-cut octagonal lantern room, standing 20 cm tall. This version uses paper clay, a cellulose-reinforced air-dry clay that resists cracking on taller forms. The finished piece is a decorative sculpture with cut window openings for interior lighting.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles. Coil-building methods referenced from V&A open-access collection for lighthouse ceramic form studies.

glossaryTerms.definition: An air-dry clay reinforced with cellulose fibres, which resists shrinkage cracking on taller or thinner forms better than standard air-dry clay
The stage at which clay holds its shape firmly but remains damp enough to join, carve, and trim
The joining method: roughen both surfaces with a needle tool, apply clay slip, then press together firmly
Fully air-dried and unfired; pale, lightweight, fragile, and ready for sealing

content.text: A lighthouse sculpture in
paper clay

is a coil-built tower topped with a slab-cut octagonal lantern room, requiring no kiln. Paper clay is the right choice for a 20 cm tall form because its cellulose fibres bridge the small cracks that standard air-dry clay develops on taller structures. The finished lighthouse stands 20 cm and has arched window cut-outs through which a tea light inside glows at night.

materials.name: Clay slip (same paper clay, thinned with water)
Acrylic paint for lighthouse stripes and lantern room (white, red, black)
Small mirror tile (optional, for lantern room floor reflector)

content.text: Preparation
Paper clay air-dry behaves like standard air-dry clay but is more forgiving on tall forms. Work slowly and build in stages: build 6-8 cm of tower height, then let that section firm at
leather-hard

before continuing upward. Building the full 20 cm height in one sitting will cause the base to collapse under the weight of soft clay above. Keep unused clay sealed in a bag between sessions. Prepare slip before starting. Roll on a canvas or cloth-covered board.
Building the tower base
Roll a flat slab 8 mm thick. Cut a circle 8 cm in diameter for the base floor. Set aside to stiffen for 20 minutes.

Roll four coils 15 mm in diameter and 25 cm long. The tower will be built from stacked coils, so consistency in coil diameter matters: roll each coil between your palms and then on the board, keeping the diameter even along the full length.
Place the first coil around the perimeter of the base circle, trimming to form a closed ring 8 cm in diameter.
Score and slip
both the base circle edge and the underside of the coil ring. Press together and blend the interior join with a wooden rib.

Add the second coil ring on top of the first: score the top of the first coil, apply slip, and press the second coil ring in place. Stagger the coil joins so no two seams align vertically. Blend the interior seam between the two coils with a wooden rib, pressing clay downward to knit them together.

Continue adding coil rings, blending each interior seam as you go. Build to a height of 7 cm, which is the first section of the tower. Leave the exterior slightly textured from the coils: this reads as stone or brick when painted later.

Allow this first section to reach leather-hard before continuing. Cover loosely with a cloth to slow drying but do not seal completely, as the clay needs to lose some moisture before taking more weight.
Building the middle and upper tower
Once the first section is leather-hard, score its top rim and add a further four coil rings. This brings the tower to 13 cm. Blend all interior seams as before.

Cut a window opening at 10 cm height: an arch 3 cm wide by 4 cm tall. Draw the arch shape with a needle tool first, then cut carefully with the fettling knife. Smooth the cut edges with a damp sponge.
Allow the second section to reach leather-hard. Then add four more coil rings to bring the tower to its full 18 cm wall height.
Gently thin the wall diameter over the final two coil rings so the top of the tower narrows slightly from 8 cm to 7 cm diameter. This gives the tower a more convincing tapered profile.
Building the lantern room
Roll a fresh slab 6 mm thick. Cut eight rectangles each 6 cm tall by 2.5 cm wide. These are the eight walls of the octagonal lantern room.

Score and slip adjacent long edges of the wall panels and join them into an octagon. Hold each join for 20 seconds. Allow the octagon to firm for 30 minutes before attempting to attach it to the tower top.
Cut a window opening in four alternating panels of the octagon: each window is 3 cm tall by 1.5 cm wide with a rectangular or arched top. These are the lantern room glazing bays.
Score and slip the base of the lantern room octagon and the top rim of the tower. Press the lantern room down onto the tower top. Blend the exterior join with a wooden rib.
Roll a small dome of clay for the lantern room roof: 4 cm in diameter, 2 cm tall. Press and blend this onto the top of the octagon.
Drying
Allow the completed lighthouse to dry at room temperature for five to seven days. Paper clay dries more slowly than standard air-dry clay. The piece passes through leather-hard and then reaches
bone-dry

when it is uniformly pale and no longer cool to the touch anywhere on the structure. Cover loosely for the first two days to slow the process and reduce cracking risk. Any fine surface cracks that appear can be filled with a paste of paper clay and water, then allowed to re-dry.
Finishing

Apply two coats of 50/50 PVA and water to all surfaces. Once the PVA is fully dry, paint with acrylics: white for the tower body, red horizontal stripes at 4 cm intervals, black for the lantern room exterior. A wash of diluted grey or brown acrylic over the coil-textured tower wall before the final white coat suggests stonework. Apply a final coat of acrylic varnish to protect the painted surface.
Care

The lighthouse is decorative only. A tea light in a metal cup can be placed inside the tower through the base opening before placing the lighthouse over it. Do not leave burning candles unattended. Keep the piece dry and dust with a soft brush rather than wiping with a damp cloth, which will soften the clay over time even when sealed.
Variations

Press a scored rope texture into the exterior coil walls at the leather-hard stage rather than leaving the coil surface plain. Use the needle tool to draw horizontal lines between coil rings, suggesting individual stone courses.
Build a small cottage at the base. Use a slab-built rectangular block, 5 cm tall. Join it to the base at leather-hard with score-and-slip. Add a pitched roof cut from two flat slab triangles.
Make a miniature version at half scale, 10 cm tall, using the same method with lighter coils rolled to 10 mm diameter. The smaller form dries faster and makes a satisfying gift-sized piece.

items.problem: Tower leaned to one side during drying
items.cause: The clay was built too tall before allowing earlier sections to firm up; soft lower walls could not support the weight
items.fix: Build in staged sections: 7 cm, allow to firm, then 6 cm more, and so on. If already leaning, press gently back to vertical at leather-hard and prop with a cylinder of crumpled newspaper

items.problem: Coil seams visible as horizontal lines on the exterior
items.cause: The exterior was not blended smooth after building
items.fix: At leather-hard, use a damp sponge to smooth the exterior. A small amount of fresh slip rubbed in and smoothed over the seam lines fills them effectively

items.problem: Window cut-out crumbled at the edges
items.cause: The clay was too soft when cut; soft clay tears rather than cuts cleanly
items.fix: Wait until the clay is at a firm leather-hard before cutting. Use a fettling knife in one clean stroke per cut rather than sawing back and forth

items.problem: Lantern room octagon did not fit the tower top
items.cause: The octagon inner diameter was too narrow or too wide for the tower outer diameter
items.fix: Measure the tower top outer diameter before cutting the lantern room wall panels. Adjust panel widths so the assembled octagon sits cleanly over the tower top

items.problem: Fine cracks appeared all over the surface during drying
items.cause: Drying too fast in a warm or draughty room
items.fix: Paper clay is more tolerant than standard air-dry, but still needs slow drying. Cover with a loose cloth and move away from heat sources. Fill surface cracks with diluted paper clay paste once leather-hard
